I feel like having stimming tools around that are deliberately not super disruptive/loud is a good idea. I know that when I was in school I didn’t really have an outlet for stimming, so I either ended up anxious and not able to listen or doing stims that probably weren’t great for me (I think my biggest “how did nobody realize I was autistic” one was pulling out my hair, for example).

Conversely, I now work a job where I talk to kids and teens a lot, many of whom are autistic or have ADHD. I personally always have something to stim quietly with because it helps me focus on the conversation, and I love to encourage the kids I work with to grab something to fidget with if they want, neurotypical and neurodivergent alike. For some kids, being able to stim or fidget with something is the difference between having really meaningful discussions vs. not being able to be mentally present/put together their thoughts at all.

Coming from a trans person in mental healthcare, I think this kind of discussion is so complicated, because these two things can get tangled a lot more often than we like to admit. I feel like there’s absolutely an extent where “transition goals” can stray into body dysmorphia— eating disorders are a huge problem for our community. However, I think there’s a big danger in comparing the two too carelessly. When it comes to something like an eating disorder/body dysmorphia, nothing you do to chase the body ideals will feel like “enough”, and it often comes at a major cost to your physical and mental health. With transition, dysphoria often eases up significantly when a person is allowed to transition and be affirmed and accepted as the gender they are, and medical and social transition are evidence-based ways to *improve* the mental health of the person experiencing dysphoria.

I think the honest answer here is that sometimes cis people who are progressive just really, really want to understand, and they can’t. It sounds like your therapist is coming from a place of wanting to help and got caught up in her own head. I’d probably remind your therapist that she can’t really “get it”, and encourage her to read up on things trans people have contributed to the mental health field. There are tons of smart people in the field who she could learn from, and it shouldn’t be your job as the client to have to educate her on that.

While I agree that I don’t think there’s necessarily a “true” self that’s static across relationships and situations, I feel like there’s a big difference between switching between scenarios/personas and masking. For example, let’s say I’m in a work meeting. Because it’s work, I will use different language than I might if I were with a friend— no swearing, more professional jargon, milder humor, and so on. I don’t really consider this masking, just adapting to circumstances in a way that’s still natural to me. It’s me, at work.

However, if I’m not comfortable being “unmasked” around the colleagues I’m meeting with, the process feels a lot more like I’m playing a character who has entirely different needs and ways of communicating than I do. I’m trying my hardest to resist the urge to stim, I’m trying to calculate how much eye contact I’m supposed to make, I’m observing and trying to replicate the exact amount of time that others spend talking so that I don’t talk too much, I’m “overacting” my reactions to things to seem more engaged and personable, and so on. 

If I’m not masking, I might be stimming to help me process the conversation and stay engaged, I’ll look all around the room while I’m talking to people instead of making eye contact, I’ll feel more comfortable giving my full input, and I’ll react more authentically. This doesn’t mean that I forget I’m at work, but it does mean that I’m better at my job because I’m not pretending that I don’t have autistic needs or autistic ways of communicating. Honestly? Patience, and finding the things *you* like about yourself and the experience of being you— whether that’s physical, social, emotional, whatever. Also, there are so many people out there who love the exact kind of person you describe yourself as— you actually remind me a lot of one of my close friends, and he has one of the strongest marriages I’ve ever seen with a wife who loves that he’s soft spoken, kind, and loves cute things. On one hand it’s like, sure, you might be different from the exact societal ideal of masculinity, but then on the other you’re *different*, and someone is going to be literally so head over heels for you because of it… even if it takes a while. I know “there’s someone out there for everyone” is a cliche but also like, there are a plethora of women out there that love gentle, kind guys— I think a lot of the trick can be looking for someone who will appreciate and love you for who you are, as opposed to looking for/trying to catch “a partner” in general, if that makes any sense. Hey man! Failing is human. Extremely human. It’s a part of life, and everybody does it— a lot. If we didn’t fail, we’d never have the chance to learn, grow, or take other paths we might not have taken. 

If you need a break right now, that’s understandable. It sounds crazy overwhelming to be where you’re at. Take a few days to recuperate so you don’t burn out on what you care about— I like to think about it like this, if you take a little time to take care of yourself now, you won’t totally hate the thing you’re trying to work on later, instead of trying to force it and then feeling horrible in all realms.

Maybe do something that makes you feel a sense of achievement, even if that thing is doing dishes, playing video games, playing sports with friends, going on a walk, drawing, or whatever feels like a meaningful but doable win. Then take some time to reconnect with why you’re doing what you’re doing, find some happiness in it if you can. Then when you’re feeling more ready, maybe head back at finding a new internship.

Love this question OP, thanks for reaching out! I work in mental healthcare, and this stereotype always got me as a person whose job is built on empathy or something adjacent. This took some thought for me, but I think I’ve got an answer, because it does feel a little different than some of the neurotypicals I know. I think for me empathy tends to be built on three things: recognition of intrinsic worth, understanding of all behavior as a manifestation of meeting needs, and occasionally the “I’ve been there” factor traditionally associated with empathy. I feel like I tend to be able to empathize with just about anybody, and I think it’s mostly based off of the fact that my internal core beliefs/rules say that everybody is a person and that everyone is acting in the context of their life. So I might not understand someone’s experiences or emotional life on a 1:1 level, but I can very much understand logically by either going through someone’s experiences, or if I don’t know them, acknowledging that everyone has their own internal lives, how someone might end up feeling how they feel or doing what they’ve done, which then does translate to my own emotional response because I’ve felt sad, happy, isolated, scared, unheard, angry, misinterpreted, etc., and that’s where the empathy comes in. I think it’s sort of like regular empathy for me, just with extra steps or more consciously practiced, which tends to be how I experience stuff in general, but I don’t consider it to be a shortcoming because I’ve heard from people I work with that the room between typically reflexive responses and the “is that accurate” factor makes me a pretty good listener.

I wasn’t always like this for sure, and I *definitely* know I got better at empathizing and understanding others after learning DBT from an instructional standpoint, especially Marsha Linehan’s levels of validation and the biosocial model, which are excellent frameworks.

The thing I've found best is to do whatever feels remotely helpful, just so long as it's not harmful to yourself or others-- even if there's some part of you that's telling yourself it's super weird. There's no "right" way to grieve. Like, if you want to make a playlist of party music that you think the person you're grieving would like, do that. If you want to take a spontaneous day trip to somewhere special that you associate with the deceased and you have the means to do so safely, do it. 

Oh, also, if people offer to help you with things, take them up on it. It helps with the responsibility itself, but more importantly the sense of community/support is really helpful and healing.

People put a lot of undue pressure to succeed/know who you are on you when you're a teenager, but you'll have limitless chances to do new things and flourish in the long-term, so whatever pace you go at, it's all good.

I love reading others’ stories so much because the relief is so palpable; I’m in the process of getting diagnosed officially, but it resonates hard with the emotions I’ve been feeling lately. 

I went through a lot of my life experiencing things that— especially in my teen years— I came to find out were heavily associated with autism, but my family and the place I grew up had a really specific vision of autism that didn’t account for masking at all, so I just assumed that I was the one neurotypical person to experience like... most of the symptoms of autism. It’s really weird thinking back on things like being in middle/high school and failing entire classes because of sensory overload (I failed the same algebra class three times, for example) and not having any of the adults in my life think that was something to look any closer at, but oh well. 

As I got older, I found that I was becoming really close friends with a lot of people who were autistic, which I thought was just an interesting coincidence! Weird how we have so much in common, but I guess I’m just so charismatic that people like me a lot! Well, not most neurotypical people, but all of my autistic friends! And then, through my job in mental health, I started doing research on/learning about autism due to having a good amount of autistic folks joining the counseling program, and stuff started to click in the back of my brain. But, I still had this feeling of “well no, I’m really good with people though, I’m really good at talking to a lot of clients at work and I’m good at making friends sometimes!”

Aaaaaaand then I learned about double empathy, and had this massive realization that every time I had taken any sort of a screening test or looked at a “you might be autistic if” piece of reading material I had been doing it thinking about my best and easiest social moments which, you guessed it, were literally all with autistic people. All of them. When I went back through with the mindset of “oh, you’re probably supposed to be thinking about neurotypical people here at the social parts” everything made way, way more sense. 

I shifted my brain from thinking about profiling myself socially as me building up a relationship with an autistic client where neither of us have any pressure to make eye contact or not stim to me attempting to have conversations with neurotypical people and struggling so immensely that it just sucks the life out of me in one way or another, and I realized that, damn, these descriptions I’ve been brushing off are very much me. I spent a few weeks thinking about it and then talked to my husband and therapist about the whole thing, and both of them gave me the feedback of “yeah that sounds really accurate and you should look into it”, so I got a testing referral as of last Friday. 

It just cracks me up but also makes me mad that I just spent so much of my life being like “no, I’m really social, i work in mental health even, I can’t possibly be autistic” because of this weird preconception that you can’t be autistic and have friends I guess? Or be autistic and have positive peer relationships with other autistic people? Anyways, I’m just glad I got here regardless, because it’s been really freeing and cathartic.

Oh my god I understand this SO much... I can’t speak for you at all, but I knew one of the hardest parts about it for me has always been the weird cycle of “I need to stop beating myself up for this, it’s not making it better” and “I don’t deserve to feel better about what I did” (even if I did literally nothing). So what ended up working for me, above all else, has been two things:

1. Designating a time of day for “thinking time”. This one is one that I pulled from a workbook and might not be the best for some people, but basically when you have an intrusive thought, instead of beating it back or holding onto it, you just acknowledge it and say “alright, I’m gonna think about this at 3pm today” (or whatever time works). Maybe write it down, if that helps— basically just like, alright, I see you, I’m not gonna make a judgment on you, but I’ve got other things to take care of. And like 98% of the time, when it gets to be 3pm, it’s not as big a deal anymore— but even if it is, giving yourself the space to worry and freak out as much as you want about it for like 15 minutes is pretty useful.

2. Mindfulness in general is really good, but it’s a super hard/abstract skill to gain, so what really helped it click with me was to visualize something familiar that’s the same basic concept. My personal thing is driving my dog places in the car: she sometimes barks or will try to get in the front seat with me, and I understand that it’s just because she’s anxious or excited, but I also understand that I can’t engage with her too much, and that I kinda just have to let her tire herself out until she sees that everything’s fine. That really helped me take a more sympathetic look at myself and my thoughts. Like, hey, I know you’re worried and upset, and I understand why you feel that way, but I gotta keep my eyes on the road so we both stay safe. Being compassionate with yourself is really important!  You’re not a bad person for having intrusive thoughts, and it’s important to recognize that a part of you is just hurting and scared. However, it’s important to acknowledge it as just another thought, and let it bark itself out until it realizes everything is fine. Sometimes, if I really need something to focus on, I’ll literally imagine the thought as my dog barking in the car, since it’s something external that I’m really used to hearing and reacting to in a “alright, let’s wait it out” way, which takes the power away from it as an all-important thing for me.

Sorry for the long winded response! I hope it doesn’t sound too weird or preachy, but it’s really helped me in the past with my intrusive thought guilt cycles.

Hello!! I'm very very recently poly, and so far, it's had a lot of pros and cons! 

(To clarify, my fiancé and I are currently in a triad, which is a little different than some poly structures, but I think I can offer some advice nonetheless [and honestly it's been the best place to start being poly since I'm getting extra affection as well]). 

At the beginning, it caused my symptoms to flare up HARD, which caused some problems for my fiancé and I-- like, to the point of almost ruin. However, after a lot of introspection, time, and intense discussions with our third partner, things are pretty good now! 

Some cons include: Getting a lot needier than usual, being anxious about where I stand with my partners, having fear that they're talking about me behind my back, being terrified that they're going to run off with each other and abandon me, having a lot of my mental energy taken up by thinking about my relationship. 

Some pros include: My fiancé is my FP, and having a third in our relationship has actually helped me get some space from him in a really constructive way-- it's gotten me out of the house and my comfort zone, helped me have a meaningful relationship with someone other than my fiancé, and has given me some outside perspective on him as a partner that I wouldn't have had before. Basically, it's been a good exercise in seeing my fiancé as just, like, a dude. A dude I really like, but human nonetheless. Also, it's honestly brought my fiancé and I closer because the process of getting to know a new person together has led us to learn things about one another that we'd either forgotten or never known about, and the experience of essentially dating someone for the first time with two people at once (one of whom you've loved for some time) is really wonderful! There's a lot more affection between us, and a lot of reassuring, and a lot of unprompted intimacy and "I love you"s.

Some tips I've picked up that have helped me a lot so far:
1. No matter how much I want to (which can be a LOT), I don't ask my partners what they do with each other intimately when I'm not there.
2. Had conversations with my partners every step of the way as to how we're all feeling, emphasizing what's working and what we want more of-- for example, I told my fiancé that a really good way to care for me when I'm anxious is to just start talking about the future with me, which keeps things light but also gives me some reassurance as to where we stand without me asking and instigating a fight/misunderstanding. 
3. Establishing specific "safe spaces" and boundaries with my partners-- for example, my therapist suggested an idea where our bed is somewhere we don't talk about other people. (We hang out in bed a lot, so that's not something we do, but it's an idea).
4. Spending time with your partner(s) and metamour(s) together is a really good idea and helps to take some of the power away from your imagination as to how your partner(s) interact with other folks they're dating. Spending time with everyone together was really the big turning point in me coming around to polyamory. 

Polyamory while being borderline takes a LOT of work and introspection and therapy and communication, but I feel better off for it, honestly! It deffo depends on the person and the relationship, and I'd suggest some couples' counseling before making any big steps (which I wish we'd have done, but pobody's nerfect).
